cases.question: Was the disappearance of the courses caused by something the student did themselves (such as accidentally dropping or deleting their course selections)?
cases.rationale: The main broad existential claim includes the actual request to the waiter; illustrative examples are not required mechanisms.

cases.question: Was the disappearance caused by the student accidentally deleting academic course selections?
cases.rationale: An explicit academic-system causal mechanism is false.

cases.question: Did the student eat a meal where the food consisted of many courses, so that by the end of the evening all courses were gone because the student had finished the food?
cases.rationale: The proposed disappearance-by-finishing mechanism is false.

cases.question: Is the story’s twist simply that the student confused the meaning of the word and all my courses were gone refers to meal courses the student ate during the evening?
cases.rationale: It invents narrator confusion and substitutes a simple eating explanation for clearing leftovers.

cases.question: Did the student physically consume some of each meal course that evening?
cases.rationale: The human clarification explicitly says each course was tasted.

cases.question: Did the student finish eating every dish?
cases.rationale: Disliked portions remained and were cleared.

cases.question: Did you submit your course selection shortly before the courses disappeared?
cases.rationale: The precise short interval is unspecified; only ordering before the meal is known.

cases.question: Were your meal preferences indicated before the deadline?
cases.rationale: Explicit reference answer.

cases.question: Did you submit your chosen dishes/menu, and the dishes all disappeared because someone else (e.g., a waiter, kitchen, or another diner) took or served them elsewhere?
cases.rationale: The waiter took them away; a broad inclusive alternative does not confirm wrong-table service.

cases.question: Did a waiter remove uneaten portions at your request because you disliked the food?
cases.rationale: The canonical causal chain.

cases.question: Did the dishes disappear because other guests ate your portions before you could have them?
cases.rationale: False replacement cause.

cases.question: Were the dishes taken away because you could not attend the dinner?
cases.rationale: The narrator arrived punctually and tasted them.

cases.question: Did staff clear the food before you could taste it?
cases.rationale: Preserves the human before/after boundary.

cases.question: Were the dishes cleared after you had tasted them but before you finished them?
cases.rationale: Tasting is not finishing; the rest was cleared.

cases.question: Did your own action cause the disappearance?
cases.rationale: The narrator actively requested removal; no academic-system modifier is present.

cases.question: Did the narrator choose food before a deadline, but finish all of it that evening?
cases.rationale: Meal preferences/deadline true; finishing everything false.

cases.question: Did the student’s failing grade result from a decision by someone other than the student and other than the course instructor (such as an administrator or committee)?
cases.rationale: The causal explanation is poor group work caused by free-riding, not a new decision-maker.

cases.question: Was the student failed because an administrator or committee overrode an otherwise passing result?
cases.rationale: False replacement mechanism.

cases.question: Was the failure caused by other people not doing their share of a heavily weighted group project?
cases.rationale: All other members free-ride.

cases.question: Was there a requirement other than tests or exams that affected the course grade?
cases.rationale: The heavily weighted group project.

cases.question: Did the student fail because a required group project was never completed?
cases.rationale: The project was completed poorly.

cases.question: Did the student complete the project but receive a poor grade because the workload was too great?
cases.rationale: The canonical causal chain.

cases.question: Did the student pass all tests and exams in this particular failed course?
cases.rationale: This course’s exact exam arrangements/results are unspecified; preserve human labels.

cases.question: Was the hidden cause an independent punitive decision by a teacher rather than poor assessed work?
cases.rationale: Ordinary grading is distinct from an arbitrary decision replacing the actual causal chain.

cases.question: Did the student complete a group project, and did every other group member contribute fairly?
cases.rationale: Completion true; other members contributing false.

cases.question: Was the decision-maker a teacher or professor after all, rather than an administrator/committee?

public_history.text: The student was officially enrolled in the course and passed all its tests and exams. However, they were not allowed to receive a passing grade in that enrolled course because an administrator or committee — not the instructor, and acting on a school policy or eligibility rule rather than on the student's coursework — made the decision that caused the fail. The passing work did not translate into credit for the enrolled course, so despite performing brilliantly, the student received a failing grade.

Did the administrator or committee fail the student because the student was taking the course via a program (such as a foreign exchange, visiting, or transfer program) that the committee ruled could not grant credit toward the student's degree?

cases.rationale: In this supplied history the player is replacing a rejected invented administrative-decision story with a teacher-decision story. Reject that replacement cause. This is not a general question about who normally marks a project.

scope: Host clarification only; opening, reference answer, rubric and existing human labels preserved. No model-generated trajectory relabeled as human.
